extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in epic poetry and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for judging whether a long poem qualifies as an epic, focusing on the fable/action (unity, completeness, greatness), appropriate length, use of episodes, and the required grandeur of parts and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable (the action) as primary consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing to be considered in an Epic Poem, is the Fable, which is perfect or imperfect according as the Action which it relates is more or less so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the poem's fable (its principal action) as the chief organizing principle for the epic; judge the poem primarily by how well that action is conceived and executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action should be but One Action (unity of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, It should be but One Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve unity by centering the poem on a single principal action; avoid making the narrative a series of disconnected actions. Examples: Homer and Virgil open at points that preserve one principal action; starting too early or too late can create multiple actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action should be an entire Action (completeness: beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondly, It should be an entire Action: An Action is entire when it is complete in all its Parts; or, as Aristotle describes it, when it consists of a Beginning, a Middle, and an End.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the action is complete and self-contained: no unrelated material before, intermixed with, or after it; do not omit any step necessary for the regular progress from origin to consummation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action should be a great Action (magnitude/significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirdly, It should be a great Action. The greatness of the action means it should be great in its Nature (consequence) and also in its Duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a subject of high consequence (e.g., the fate of a people or species rather than only individuals). The epic's stakes should be large in moral, cosmic, or historical import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness of parts and principal members
rubrics_metrics.description: In Poetry, as in Architecture, not only the Whole, but the principal Members, and every Part of them, should be Great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each major episode, character, and component should possess dignity and grandeur appropriate to an epic—avoid trivial or petty elements in principal scenes and persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due length (duration) proportionate to memory and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle... does not only mean that it should be great in its Nature, but also in its Duration... The just Measure of this kind of Magnitude, he explains by the Similitude [too short is lost; too long overcharges memory].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance extension and compression: too short an action will not register distinctly in the reader's memory; too long will overburden it. Use episodes and ornamentation to expand an action to a satisfying length without excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Episodes and Machinery to enrich without breaking unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes are allowable and useful when they naturally arise from the Subject; Milton cast earlier events into books by way of Episode to preserve unity. Episodes should run parallel with the great Action and can add variety and simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ episodes and mythic machinery to diversify and extend the narrative, but ensure they relate closely to and illuminate the central action (counterparts/copies are effective). Avoid extraneous episodes that fracture the poem's unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin in the midst of things (in medias res) to preserve unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer to preserve the Unity of his Action hastens into the Midst of Things... He therefore opens his Poem with the Discord of his Princes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting the epic 'in the middle' can help focus on the principal action; earlier or much later starting points risk creating multiple actions or diluting unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain natural order of parts as they grow out of one another
rubrics_metrics.description: The Parts of it are told in the most distinct Manner, and grow out of one another in the most natural Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize episodes so each follows logically from the previous, producing a natural progression from cause to effect that supports the completeness of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend a short action by invention cautiously (respect source constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: It was easier for Homer and Virgil to dash the Truth with Fiction... but Milton, having few Traditions and religious restraints, proceeded with caution; yet filled his Story with surprising Incidents analogous to Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the source material is limited or sacred, invent with care—ensure added incidents bear close analogy to authoritative sources and will not offend scrupulous readers; embellishments should harmonize with the subject's nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: No determinable temporal bounds for epic action
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the Criticks... having laid down Rules to circumscribe the Action of an Epic Poem with any determin'd Number of Years, Days or Hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge an epic by a set clock or fixed span of years; appropriate temporal scope depends on subject and how well the poem balances variety and unity for reader memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization by concrete habits and small details
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are made evident through particular habits and outward signs (example: Irus's affectation of closeness, choice of dress to appear older, counting money morning and evening, refusing visitors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal character through concrete, repeated actions and material details rather than abstract statement—use dress, routine, gestures, and social interactions to make psychology credible and amusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of letters and mimicry as a rhetorical device
rubrics_metrics.description: The author prints letters and remarks on a correspondent's excellent Faculty in Mimickry; forged letters and imitated voices are used to amuse and diversify the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate letters, different voices, and acts of mimicry to vary perspective, lend authenticity, and create comic or satirical effects; ensure such devices align with authorial tone and do not obscure the main action.
